metadata.title: Revisiting educational assumptions: The surprising negative link between creative extracurricular activities and creative thinking in PISA 2022

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 creative thinking data with a complex, multi-stage sampling design and planned missingness. For the analytic models, the authors applied the whole-sample student/sampling weight to obtain population-representative estimates and used 80 replicate weights to estimate sampling variance and standard errors under the PISA design. Regression and correlation analyses were conducted with R survey-weighting tools (weights package for weighted correlations; survey package for regression) to incorporate stratification/cluster structure. The paper does not report a specific weight variable name in the provided text, but it explicitly states the use of whole-sample weights and 80 replicate weights; therefore, analysts should use the corresponding PISA 2022 student weight and replicate weights from the OECD database when reproducing results.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis uses PISA 2022 creative thinking assessment data, where about 28% of sampled students were assigned the creative thinking assessment. The authors excluded countries that did not meet OECD sampling guidelines for result interpretation (combined school-level and within-school exclusions >5%, final weighted school response rate <85%, or student response rate <80%). They further restricted to countries with data relevant to the study and to students with available data for the creative thinking outcome and the included predictors; the regression table note reports listwise deletion, yielding an analytic sample of 230,951 students after excluding cases with missing data. The creative thinking outcome is based on plausible values (10 PVs) for students who encountered the creative thinking domain, while other students’ PVs are represented in the dataset via the PISA conditioning model.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (15-year-olds; creative thinking domain; plausible values)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Weighted Pearson correlations (Rubin's rules across 10 PVs): r = −0.25 (inside school), r = −0.32 (outside school). Survey-weighted regression (Rubin's rules across 10 PVs): pseudo-R² = 0.54 (deviance-based), variance-based R² = 0.27. Standardized regression coefficients: Activities outside school β = −0.27 (SE = 0.01, p < .001); Activities inside school β = −0.06 (SE = 0.01, p < .001). Interaction effects: outside-school × openness β = 0.03 (p < .001) and outside-school × self-efficacy β = 0.04 (p < .001); inside-school × feeling safe β = 0.01 (p = 0.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 creative thinking plausible values the study leveraged creative activities inside and outside school together with SES, gender, immigrant background, creative self-efficacy, openness to intellect, and feeling safe to predict creative thinking performance, finding that both inside- and outside-school creative activities were negative predictors overall (β = −0.06 and β = −0.27, respectively) while specific psychological moderators (openness to intellect and creative self-efficacy for outside-school activities) reversed the negative relation in small but significant ways. This indicates that simply increasing students’ engagement in creative extracurricular activities may not improve measured creative thinking unless activity formats and student readiness (e.g., openness and self-efficacy) are aligned with how the assessment operationalizes creativity, though the effects are small and secondary-analysis constraints of PV conditioning apply.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2022 creative thinking assessment data for 15-year-olds across 49 countries (final analytic sample N = 372,193 for the PV-based dataset; regression analytic sample after listwise deletion N = 230,951). The creative thinking outcome is based on 10 plausible values, which the authors aggregated using Rubin’s rules, and the models incorporate PISA’s complex sampling design via whole-sample student weights and 80 replicate weights. Weighted Pearson correlations show negative associations between creative thinking and creative activities both inside (r = −0.25) and outside school (r = −0.32), and survey-weighted regression yields negative standardized effects for activities inside (β = −0.06) and outside school (β = −0.27), with pseudo-R² = 0.54 and variance-based R² = 0.27. Moderation analyses indicate that openness to intellect and creative self-efficacy weaken or reverse the negative relation for outside-school activities, while feeling safe weakly moderates inside-school activities. Limitations include small effect sizes, reliance on PVs generated from a conditioning model (limiting novel causal pathways), and the use of listwise deletion for missing predictor/outcome data.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The paper is an empirical correlational/regression analysis using PISA plausible values and survey-weighted inference, not a machine-learning predictive modeling study. Consequently, no ML algorithms are evaluated or compared, so ml_techniques.all_techniques is empty and ml_techniques.primary is left null. The extraction still captures the substantive statistical results (correlations, survey-weighted regression coefficients, and interactions) as the main findings.
